He saw painting as a philosophical and scientific pursuit, stating, “Painting is a science and all sciences are founded on mathematics, and cannot be exact without mathematics.” This blend of empirical observation and mathematical understanding became the bedrock upon which the luminous realism of Renaissance painting was built.

Linear Perspective: The Foundation of Illusionary Space

Perhaps the most revolutionary scientific advancement in Renaissance painting was the development of linear perspective. Credited largely to the architect Filippo Brunelleschi in the early 15th century, and later codified by Leon Battista Alberti in his treatise De Pictura (1435), linear perspective offered artists a mathematical method to create the illusion of three-dimensional space on a two-dimensional surface.

The core principle of linear perspective involves the use of a vanishing point, a single point on the horizon line towards which all parallel lines in a scene appear to recede. For a detailed explanation of linear perspective, refer to Wikipedia's entry on Perspective (graphical).

The creation of such convincing illusionary spaces often required an understanding of spatial relationships that mirrored an architect's or engineer's perspective. For more on how such historical advancements inform contemporary practice, see our article on Reading Art History as a Practicing Artist.
